title: The CIA triad and security goals
objective: Compare and contrast the core security concepts that every other topic builds on.

questions.q: What does the "C" in the CIA triad stand for?
options: Confidentiality — data is seen only by those authorized
questions.explain: CIA = Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability. It is the foundation of every security decision.

questions.q: Encrypting a hard drive primarily protects which part of the CIA triad?
questions.explain: Encryption stops unauthorized reading. Hashing protects integrity; backups and redundancy protect availability.

questions.q: A hash value is used to verify that a file has not changed. Which goal is this?
questions.explain: If the hash still matches, the data is intact. A changed byte changes the hash.

questions.q: Which concept ensures a sender cannot later deny sending a message?
questions.explain: Digital signatures provide non-repudiation because only the sender holds the private key.

questions.q: A DDoS attack most directly threatens which security goal?
questions.explain: Flooding a service so real users cannot reach it is an availability attack.

questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do
Authorization proves identity; authentication grants access
questions.explain: You authenticate (log in), then the system authorizes (checks permissions).

questions.q: Which term describes the assurance that a system or data is available when needed?
questions.explain: Achieved with redundancy, backups, failover and DDoS protection.

questions.q: In AAA, what does the third A (Accounting) provide?
options: A record of what a user did, for auditing
questions.explain: Authentication, Authorization, Accounting — logs and audit trails are the accounting piece.

questions.q: On Linux, generate a SHA-256 hash of the file report.pdf to check its integrity.
questions.explain: Compare the value later; a single changed bit produces a completely different hash.

labs.title: Prove integrity with hashing
labs.scenario: Create a file, hash it, change one character, and hash it again to see the value change completely.
verify: the two hashes are completely different

labs.title: Map controls to the CIA triad
labs.scenario: For each control, write down which CIA goal it mainly serves: full-disk encryption, RAID, a load balancer, a digital signature, a firewall rule blocking a port, a daily backup.
hints: One control can serve more than one goal, but pick the primary.
steps: # digital signature / file hash -> Integrity (and signatures add non-repudiation)
verify: you can justify each mapping in one sentence

labs.title: Spot the goal being attacked
labs.scenario: For each scenario name the CIA goal harmed: (a) ransomware encrypts your files, (b) an attacker reads your email, (c) a hacker alters a bank balance.
steps: # (a) Availability (you can't reach your data) -- and Confidentiality if copied
verify: you can explain each choice

title: Security control types
objective: Categorise controls by type (technical, managerial, operational, physical) and function (preventive, detective, corrective, etc.).

questions.q: A firewall is which control TYPE?
questions.explain: Technical controls are enforced by technology. A security policy is managerial; a guard is physical.

questions.q: A written security policy is which control type?
questions.explain: Managerial controls are the policies and procedures that direct the security program.

questions.q: Security guards, fences and locks are which control type?
questions.explain: Physical controls protect the tangible world — buildings, hardware, people.

questions.q: A backup is which control FUNCTION?
options: Corrective — it restores after an incident
questions.explain: Corrective controls fix or recover. Backups let you recover from ransomware or hardware failure.

questions.q: Motion-sensor lights and warning signs are which control function?
options: Deterrent — they discourage an attacker from trying
questions.explain: A deterrent influences behaviour; a preventive control actually blocks the action.

questions.q: Which control function is an intrusion DETECTION system (IDS)?
questions.explain: An IDS alerts you that something happened. An IPS that blocks it is preventive.

questions.q: What is a compensating control?
options: An alternative control used when the primary control is not feasible
A control that pays for damages
A control that replaces all others permanently
questions.explain: Example: if you cannot patch a legacy server, you isolate it on its own VLAN as a compensating control.

questions.q: A door lock is which control function?
questions.explain: It prevents unauthorized entry. A camera that records entry would be detective.

labs.title: Classify controls two ways
labs.scenario: For each item give both its TYPE and its FUNCTION: antivirus software, a CCTV camera, an incident-response plan, a bollard, encryption, a re-imaging procedure.
verify: you can defend each pair

labs.title: Choose a compensating control
labs.scenario: A vendor app requires an outdated TLS version you cannot fix. List three compensating controls to reduce the risk.
steps: # isolate the server on its own VLAN with strict firewall rules
# put it behind a reverse proxy that terminates modern TLS
# increase monitoring/logging and restrict who can reach it
verify: each control reduces exposure without changing the app

title: Change management and zero trust
objective: Explain the importance of change management and the zero-trust model.

questions.q: Why does security care about change management?
options: Unplanned or untracked changes are a top cause of outages and new vulnerabilities
It replaces the need for backups
It is only about software licensing
questions.explain: Formal change control means changes are reviewed, approved, tested and reversible.

questions.q: What is a "rollback plan" in change management?
options: A documented way to undo a change if it causes problems
A plan to attack a rolled-out system
questions.explain: Never deploy a change you cannot back out of.

questions.q: In the zero-trust model, what is the core principle?
options: Never trust, always verify — every request is authenticated and authorized regardless of location
Trust remote users more than local users
questions.explain: Zero trust removes the idea of a trusted internal network.

questions.q: In zero-trust terms, what is the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)?
options: The component that actually allows or blocks the request
questions.explain: The Policy Decision Point (PDP) decides; the PEP enforces the decision.

questions.q: What does "least privilege" mean?
options: Give each user or process only the access it needs to do its job
Remove all access by default forever
questions.explain: It limits the damage a compromised account can do.

questions.q: What is microsegmentation?
options: Dividing the network into small zones so a breach in one cannot spread freely
Splitting a hard disk into partitions
Using smaller subnets for Wi-Fi only
questions.explain: It supports zero trust by limiting lateral movement.

questions.q: Why is a "maintenance window" used?
options: To make disruptive changes at a planned low-impact time with approvals in place
questions.explain: Changes outside approved windows are a red flag.

questions.q: On Linux, show the last changes made to a Git-tracked config repo (change history).
questions.explain: Version control is a simple, powerful change-management tool for configs.

labs.title: Design a change request
labs.scenario: Write a one-page change request to upgrade a production web server's TLS: include purpose, risk, backout/rollback plan, test plan, and approval step.
steps: # Risk: old clients may fail; mitigation: notify + test
# Rollback: keep old config file, restore + restart on failure
# Test: staging server first, then curl -v to confirm TLS 1.3
# Approval: change advisory board sign-off, maintenance window
verify: the request could actually be approved and reversed

labs.title: Apply least privilege
labs.scenario: On a Linux box, find a service running as root that should not, and describe how to run it as a dedicated low-privilege user instead.
steps: ps -eo user,comm | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
# create a service account:  useradd -r -s /sbin/nologin appsvc
# set the unit's User=appsvc and restrict its file permissions
verify: the service no longer needs root

title: Threat actors and motivations
objective: Compare threat actors, their attributes and motivations.

questions.q: Which threat actor typically has the most resources and patience?
questions.explain: Advanced Persistent Threats are well-funded and pursue long-term goals like espionage.

questions.q: A "script kiddie" is best described as:
options: An unskilled attacker using tools written by others
questions.explain: Low skill, low resources, but still dangerous with off-the-shelf tools.

questions.q: What primarily motivates a hacktivist?
questions.explain: Hacktivists deface sites or leak data to make a statement.

questions.q: Which term describes a trusted employee who intentionally causes harm?
questions.explain: Insiders are dangerous because they already have access and knowledge.

questions.q: What is "shadow IT"?
options: Hardware or software used inside an organization without IT approval
questions.explain: Shadow IT (like an unapproved cloud app) creates unmanaged risk.

questions.q: Which attacker attribute describes whether they are inside or outside the organization?
questions.explain: Actor attributes include internal/external, resources/funding, and level of sophistication.

questions.q: An organized crime group's usual motivation is:
questions.explain: They run ransomware and fraud operations for money.

questions.q: What is threat intelligence used for?
options: Understanding likely attackers and their techniques to prepare defenses
questions.explain: Feeds and reports (e.g., MITRE ATT&CK) map real-world adversary behavior.

labs.title: Build a threat-actor profile
labs.scenario: For your own scenario (a small online shop), list the two most likely threat actors, their motivation, capability, and one control that raises their cost.
steps: # e.g. organized crime -> money -> ransomware -> offline backups + MFA
# e.g. script kiddie -> notoriety -> automated scans -> patching + WAF
verify: each actor has a matching control

labs.title: Explore MITRE ATT&CK
labs.scenario: Open attack.mitre.org and pick one technique (e.g., Phishing). Note its ID, one detection idea, and one mitigation.
hints: You can browse it read-only; no account needed.
steps: # e.g. T1566 Phishing -> detect: email gateway + user reports
#                    -> mitigate: user training, link rewriting, MFA
verify: you can name a real technique ID and a defense

title: Social engineering
objective: Explain common social-engineering techniques and why they work.

questions.q: What is phishing?
options: Fraudulent messages that trick users into revealing data or clicking malicious links
questions.explain: Phishing is the most common initial attack vector.

questions.q: "Spear phishing" differs from phishing because it is:
options: Targeted at a specific person or organization with personalized detail
questions.explain: Whaling is spear phishing aimed at executives ("big fish").

questions.q: An attacker calls pretending to be IT support to get a password. This is:
questions.explain: Smishing uses SMS; vishing uses voice calls.

questions.q: Following an employee through a secure door without badging in is:
questions.explain: A physical social-engineering attack. Mantraps and turnstiles reduce it.

questions.q: What is "pretexting"?
options: Inventing a believable scenario to gain trust and information
questions.explain: "I'm from the bank's fraud team..." is a pretext.

questions.q: Which principle explains why urgency works in scams ("Act now or your account closes")?
options: Urgency/scarcity pressure that bypasses careful thinking
questions.explain: Attackers exploit authority, urgency, familiarity, and fear.

questions.q: A "watering hole" attack means:
options: Compromising a website the target group is known to visit
questions.explain: The attacker waits for victims at a site they trust.

questions.q: What is the best single defense against social engineering?
options: Security-awareness training combined with verification procedures
questions.explain: People are the target, so people must be trained and given a way to verify.

labs.title: Analyze a phishing email
labs.scenario: Take a suspicious email (real or sample) and list five red flags an analyst would flag.
steps: # mismatched sender domain, generic greeting, urgent threat,
# link text not matching the real URL (hover to check),
# unexpected attachment, spelling errors, request for credentials
verify: you found at least five indicators

labs.title: Inspect a link safely
labs.scenario: Without clicking, reveal where a shortened or masked link really points, using the terminal.
hints: curl -sI follows headers; use -L to see redirects, but stop before loading content.
steps: # or expand a shortener:  curl -sI https://bit.ly/xxxx | grep -i location
verify: you can state the real destination host

labs.title: Report-and-verify drill
labs.scenario: Write the 3-step procedure a user should follow when they suspect a phishing message.
steps: # 3. Verify any request through a known official channel
verify: the steps stop the attack and preserve evidence

title: Malware types
objective: Compare types of malware and how they spread.

questions.q: What defines a virus versus a worm?
options: A virus needs a host file/user action to spread; a worm self-propagates across networks
A worm needs a host; a virus spreads itself
questions.explain: Worms spread on their own (e.g., across a LAN); viruses attach to files.

questions.q: Ransomware primarily does what?
options: Encrypts or locks data and demands payment to restore access
questions.explain: Best defenses: offline/immutable backups, patching, MFA, least privilege.

questions.q: A "Trojan" is malware that:
options: Disguises itself as legitimate software to trick the user into running it
questions.explain: Named after the Trojan horse — it looks useful but carries a payload.

questions.q: Software that secretly records keystrokes is a:
questions.explain: It captures passwords and messages. It can be software or hardware.

questions.q: A rootkit is dangerous mainly because it:
options: Hides itself and gains privileged, persistent control of the OS
questions.explain: Rootkits operate at a low level, hiding processes and files from tools.

questions.q: A "logic bomb" triggers when:
options: A specific condition or time is met (e.g., a date, or a user being deleted)
questions.explain: A disgruntled admin might set code to fire after they are removed from payroll.

questions.q: Fileless malware is hard to detect because it:
options: Runs in memory using legitimate tools (like PowerShell) rather than dropping a file
questions.explain: Living-off-the-land techniques abuse built-in binaries.

questions.q: What is a botnet?
options: A network of compromised devices controlled by an attacker
questions.explain: Bots (zombies) take orders from a command-and-control (C2) server, often for DDoS.

questions.q: On Linux, hash a suspicious binary so you can check it against threat-intel feeds.
questions.explain: Submit the hash (not the file) to a reputation service like an IOC lookup.

labs.title: Malware indicator triage
labs.scenario: You find these on a host: a new scheduled task, a process with no file on disk, outbound traffic to a strange IP every 60s, and a renamed powershell.exe. Match each to a malware behavior.
steps: # process with no file -> fileless / in-memory
verify: each indicator maps to a technique

labs.title: Safe static look at a file
labs.scenario: Without executing it, gather basic facts about a suspicious file: type, size, and readable strings.
verify: you can describe the file without running it

title: Password and application attacks
objective: Explain password attacks, injection and other application attacks.

questions.q: A brute-force password attack:
options: Tries every possible combination until one works
Uses a list of common passwords only
questions.explain: A dictionary attack uses a wordlist; brute force is exhaustive; both are slower with strong hashes and lockouts.

questions.q: What is a dictionary attack?
options: Trying passwords from a list of likely words/leaked passwords
questions.explain: Wordlists like rockyou.txt are common in labs.

questions.q: Why does "salting" a password hash help?
options: It adds random data so identical passwords hash differently, defeating precomputed tables
questions.explain: Salt defeats rainbow tables and stops attackers from seeing duplicate passwords.

questions.q: SQL injection works by:
options: Inserting malicious SQL through input that the app runs against its database
questions.explain: Parameterized queries (prepared statements) are the main defense.

questions.q: Cross-site scripting (XSS) allows an attacker to:
options: Run malicious script in another user's browser via a vulnerable web page
questions.explain: Output encoding and a Content Security Policy mitigate XSS.

questions.q: A "pass-the-hash" attack means:
options: Authenticating with a stolen password hash without cracking it
questions.explain: It abuses how some protocols accept the hash as proof of identity.

questions.q: What is credential stuffing?
options: Reusing username/password pairs leaked from one site against many others
questions.explain: It works because people reuse passwords; MFA stops most of it.

questions.q: A race condition (TOCTOU) vulnerability is:
options: A flaw where the state changes between the time of check and time of use
Two users logging in at once safely
questions.explain: Attackers exploit the tiny window between a check and an action.

questions.q: On Linux, generate a bcrypt-style password hash to see how modern hashing looks.
questions.explain: -6 is SHA-512 crypt with a random salt; note the different output each run.

labs.title: Compare hash strength
labs.scenario: Hash the same password with an old fast algorithm and a modern salted one; explain which is harder to crack and why.
steps: openssl passwd -6 "password123"    # note: different salt -> different output
verify: you can explain salting and slow hashing

labs.title: Prevent SQL injection (concept lab)
labs.scenario: Given the unsafe query   "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + input + "'"   rewrite it as a parameterized query and explain why it stops injection.
steps: # unsafe: input   ' OR '1'='1   returns all rows
# safe (pseudo):  db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", [input])
# the input is treated as data, never as SQL code
verify: the injection payload no longer changes the query logic

labs.title: Account-lockout defense
labs.scenario: Describe the settings that turn a brute-force attack from easy to impractical.
steps: # account lockout after N failed attempts
verify: an attacker cannot try enough guesses in time

title: Network attacks
objective: Explain common network-based attacks.

questions.q: A man-in-the-middle (on-path) attack lets an attacker:
options: Intercept and possibly alter traffic between two parties
questions.explain: Defenses: TLS everywhere, certificate validation, and secure Wi-Fi.

questions.q: ARP poisoning is used to:
options: Trick devices into sending traffic to the attacker on a local network
questions.explain: The attacker maps their MAC to another host's IP. Dynamic ARP inspection helps.

questions.q: DNS poisoning (spoofing) results in:
options: Users being sent to a malicious IP for a legitimate domain name
questions.explain: DNSSEC and using trusted resolvers reduce it.

questions.q: A SYN flood is a type of:
options: Denial-of-service attack that exhausts a server's half-open connections
questions.explain: SYN cookies and rate limiting mitigate it.

questions.q: What is a "distributed" denial of service (DDoS)?
options: A DoS launched from many compromised sources at once
questions.explain: A botnet amplifies the flood; cloud scrubbing services help absorb it.

questions.q: Rogue access point vs evil twin: the evil twin specifically:
options: Impersonates a legitimate AP's name (SSID) to trick users into connecting
questions.explain: Both are dangerous; the evil twin mimics a trusted network.

questions.q: A replay attack succeeds when:
options: Captured valid data (like an auth token) is resent to impersonate a user
The network is replayed on video
questions.explain: Timestamps, nonces and session tokens prevent replay.

questions.q: DNS over HTTPS (DoH) mainly improves:
options: Privacy/integrity of DNS queries by encrypting them
questions.explain: It stops on-path snooping and tampering of DNS lookups.

questions.q: On Linux, capture the first 20 packets on interface eth0 to inspect traffic (authorized lab only).
questions.explain: Only capture on networks you own or are authorized to test.

labs.title: Read a capture for plaintext
labs.scenario: On your own lab network, capture traffic to an HTTP (not HTTPS) test site and show why HTTPS matters.
steps: # observe that HTTP headers and data are readable
verify: you can see plaintext over HTTP and explain how TLS fixes it

labs.title: Detect ARP spoofing
labs.scenario: Show your ARP table and explain what a duplicated MAC for two IPs (or the gateway MAC changing) would indicate.
steps: # two IPs sharing one MAC, or the gateway's MAC suddenly changing = possible ARP poisoning
verify: you can spot a suspicious ARP entry

title: Vulnerabilities and the attack surface
objective: Explain hardware, software and cloud vulnerabilities.

questions.q: A "zero-day" vulnerability is one that:
options: Has no patch available because the vendor does not yet know or has not fixed it
questions.explain: Defense relies on layered controls and behavior-based detection.

questions.q: What is the difference between a vulnerability and an exploit?
options: A vulnerability is the weakness; an exploit is the code/technique that abuses it
questions.explain: A vulnerability with no working exploit is lower (but not zero) risk.

questions.q: "Patch management" reduces risk by:
options: Applying vendor updates that fix known vulnerabilities in a controlled way
questions.explain: Unpatched systems are one of the most common breach causes.

questions.q: A buffer overflow happens when:
options: A program writes more data than a memory buffer can hold, corrupting adjacent memory
questions.explain: It can let an attacker run their own code. Modern OSes use ASLR/DEP to mitigate.

questions.q: "Legacy" systems are risky because they:
options: No longer receive security updates and may run outdated protocols
questions.explain: If they cannot be replaced, isolate them (compensating control).

questions.q: Misconfiguration is dangerous because it:
options: Leaves systems exposed even when the software itself is secure (e.g., open S3 bucket)
questions.explain: Secure baselines and configuration reviews catch these.

questions.q: A supply-chain attack targets:
options: A trusted vendor/component to reach that vendor's many customers
questions.explain: Example: malware inserted into a software update.

questions.q: What is "TTPs" in threat analysis?
options: Tactics, Techniques and Procedures — how an adversary operates
questions.explain: TTPs (from MITRE ATT&CK) help defenders anticipate behavior.

questions.q: On Linux, list installed packages so you can check them against a vulnerability list.
questions.explain: Feed the versions into a scanner or CVE lookup to find known issues.

labs.title: Reduce your attack surface
labs.scenario: On a Linux server, list listening services and disable one that is not needed.
steps: ss -tulpn        # confirm the port is gone
verify: fewer ports are open than before

labs.title: Prioritize with CVSS (concept)
labs.scenario: Two findings: (a) CVSS 9.8 internet-facing RCE, (b) CVSS 4.3 local info-leak on an isolated box. Which do you patch first and why?
steps: # (a) first: higher severity AND exposed to the internet
# (b) later: low severity and not reachable by attackers
verify: you can justify prioritizing by severity + exposure

title: Secure network design
objective: Compare architecture concepts: segmentation, DMZ, defense in depth.

questions.q: What is a DMZ (screened subnet)?
options: A network zone between the internet and the internal LAN for public-facing servers
questions.explain: Web/email servers sit in the DMZ so a breach there does not directly reach the LAN.

questions.q: "Defense in depth" means:
options: Using multiple layers of controls so one failure does not cause a breach
questions.explain: If one layer fails, others still protect the asset.

questions.q: A VLAN provides:
options: Logical segmentation of a switch into separate broadcast domains
questions.explain: VLANs separate traffic (e.g., guests from staff) without extra cabling.

questions.q: What does a jump server (bastion host) do?
options: Provides a single, hardened, monitored entry point to manage internal systems
questions.explain: Admins connect to the jump host first; direct admin access elsewhere is blocked.

questions.q: Which describes an air-gapped system?
options: A system physically isolated from other networks
questions.explain: Used for the most sensitive systems; data crosses only via strict manual processes.

questions.q: A proxy server placed between users and the internet can:
options: Filter, cache and log outbound web requests
questions.explain: A forward proxy controls client access; a reverse proxy protects servers.

questions.q: What is a "honeypot"?
options: A decoy system designed to attract and study attackers
questions.explain: It has no production value, so any interaction is suspicious.

questions.q: Network Access Control (NAC) enforces:
options: Health/identity checks before a device is allowed onto the network
questions.explain: A device failing posture checks can be quarantined to a remediation VLAN.

questions.q: On Linux, view the routing table to understand how traffic leaves this host.
questions.explain: Segmentation and gateways show up here as different routes.

labs.title: Segment a small network (design)
labs.scenario: Design VLANs for a small office: staff, guests, servers, IoT cameras. State which segments may talk to which.
steps: # VLAN10 staff, VLAN20 guests (internet only), VLAN30 servers, VLAN40 IoT
# guests -> internet only; IoT -> no internet, no staff; staff -> servers on needed ports
verify: no segment has more access than it needs

labs.title: Build a host firewall baseline
labs.scenario: On a Linux server, allow only SSH and HTTPS inbound and confirm.
verify: only 22 and 443 are reachable

title: Cloud and virtualization security
objective: Summarize secure cloud and virtualization concepts.

questions.q: In the cloud shared-responsibility model, who secures the physical data center?
questions.explain: The customer always owns their data and access; the split depends on IaaS/PaaS/SaaS.

questions.q: In IaaS, patching the guest operating system is usually:
questions.explain: IaaS gives you the VM; you secure the OS and apps.

questions.q: What is a CASB?
options: A Cloud Access Security Broker that enforces policy between users and cloud apps
questions.explain: It gives visibility and control over SaaS usage (including shadow IT).

questions.q: "VM escape" is dangerous because it:
options: Lets code break out of a guest VM to the hypervisor/host
questions.explain: It breaks the isolation that virtualization relies on.

questions.q: What does "infrastructure as code" (IaC) improve for security?
options: Consistent, reviewable, version-controlled configuration of infrastructure
questions.explain: Misconfigurations can be caught in code review before deployment.

questions.q: A "container" differs from a VM because it:
options: Shares the host kernel and packages just the app and its dependencies
Includes a full separate OS kernel
questions.explain: Containers are lighter but share the kernel, so kernel isolation matters.

questions.q: Which is a key control for securing cloud storage buckets?
options: Blocking public access and enforcing least-privilege IAM policies
questions.explain: Public buckets are a classic breach source.

questions.q: Serverless (functions) shifts more responsibility to the provider but you still own:
questions.explain: Over-privileged functions and hard-coded secrets are the common risks.

questions.q: With the AWS CLI, list S3 buckets to review what exists (authorized account only).
questions.explain: Then check each bucket's public-access and policy settings.

labs.title: Classify cloud responsibilities
labs.scenario: For SaaS, PaaS and IaaS, state who patches the OS, who secures the app, and who owns the data.
steps: # IaaS: customer patches OS + app; provider does hardware/hypervisor
# PaaS: provider patches OS/runtime; customer secures app + data
# SaaS: provider does almost all; customer manages data + access/config
verify: you can fill the responsibility matrix

labs.title: Harden a container image (concept)
labs.scenario: List four things you would change to harden a Dockerfile that currently runs as root and installs everything.
steps: # create and run as a non-root user (USER appsvc)
# install only needed packages, pin versions
# scan the image for CVEs before push; don't bake in secrets
verify: the image is smaller, non-root, and scanned

title: Cryptography concepts
objective: Compare symmetric/asymmetric crypto, hashing and PKI basics.

questions.q: Symmetric encryption uses:
options: The same key to encrypt and decrypt
A public and a private key
questions.explain: Fast (e.g., AES) but you must share the key securely.

questions.q: Asymmetric encryption uses:
options: A public key to encrypt and a matching private key to decrypt
questions.explain: RSA and ECC are examples. Slower, so often used to exchange a symmetric key.

questions.q: To send a confidential message to Bob, Alice encrypts with:
options: Bob's public key (only Bob's private key can decrypt)
questions.explain: Anyone can hold the public key; only Bob holds the private key.

questions.q: A digital signature is created by:
options: Encrypting a hash of the message with the sender's private key
Encrypting with the receiver's public key
questions.explain: The receiver verifies with the sender's public key — proving integrity and origin.

questions.q: What does a Certificate Authority (CA) do?
options: Issues and vouches for digital certificates that bind a public key to an identity
questions.explain: Browsers trust certificates signed by trusted CAs.

questions.q: Hashing is different from encryption because it is:
options: One-way — you cannot reverse a hash back to the original
questions.explain: Hashing verifies integrity; encryption protects confidentiality (and is reversible with the key).

questions.q: "Perfect forward secrecy" ensures:
options: A compromised long-term key does not expose past session keys
questions.explain: Each session uses ephemeral keys (e.g., ECDHE).

questions.q: What is the purpose of a certificate's CRL or OCSP?
options: To check whether a certificate has been revoked before trusting it
questions.explain: A revoked (e.g., stolen) certificate must not be trusted even if unexpired.

questions.q: Create a self-signed certificate and key for a lab web server.
questions.explain: Self-signed is fine for labs; production uses a trusted CA.

labs.title: Encrypt and decrypt a file (symmetric)
labs.scenario: Use OpenSSL to encrypt a file with AES, then decrypt it, proving symmetric crypto works.
verify: the decrypted file equals the original

labs.title: Sign and verify (asymmetric)
labs.scenario: Generate a key pair, sign a file, and verify the signature.
verify: verification prints "Verified OK"

labs.title: Inspect a real certificate
labs.scenario: View the certificate a website presents and note its issuer, validity dates, and key size.
steps: openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -dates -subject
verify: you can read the issuer and expiry

title: Identity and access management
objective: Explain IAM, authentication factors and access-control models.

questions.q: The three authentication factor categories are:
options: Something you know, something you have, something you are
questions.explain: Add location ("somewhere you are") and behavior as extra factors.

questions.q: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires factors from:
questions.explain: A password + PIN is still one category ("know"), so it is not true MFA.

questions.q: In RBAC, access is granted based on:
questions.explain: Role-Based Access Control scales better than assigning rights per user.

questions.q: ABAC grants access based on:
options: Attributes (user, resource, action, environment) evaluated by policy
questions.explain: Attribute-Based Access Control is flexible (e.g., "managers, on the corporate network, during work hours").

questions.q: In Mandatory Access Control (MAC), access decisions are:
options: Enforced by the system using labels/clearances, not changeable by users
questions.explain: SELinux is a MAC implementation. Users cannot override the labels.

questions.q: Discretionary Access Control (DAC) means:
options: The resource owner decides who gets access
questions.explain: Standard Linux file permissions (chmod) are DAC.

questions.q: Single Sign-On (SSO) improves security by:
options: Letting users authenticate once to reach many services, reducing password reuse
Removing the need for passwords entirely
Making one account admin of all
questions.explain: Federation (SAML/OIDC) enables SSO across organizations.

questions.q: What is the principle behind "just-in-time" (JIT) privileged access?
options: Elevated rights are granted only when needed and for a limited time
questions.explain: It shrinks the window an attacker can abuse standing privileges.

questions.q: On Linux, show which groups a user belongs to (their role memberships).
questions.explain: Group membership is how RBAC is often implemented on Linux.

labs.title: Enforce MFA thinking
labs.scenario: For each login method, say whether it is true MFA: (a) password + SMS code, (b) password + security question, (c) fingerprint + hardware token, (d) PIN + password.
verify: you can classify each correctly

labs.title: Implement least-privilege roles
labs.scenario: On a Linux host, create a "backupops" group, add a user, and give that group (not the user) read access to /var/backups.
verify: the user gets access only through the role/group

labs.title: Time-based access (concept)
labs.scenario: Describe how you would restrict a contractor account so it only works Mon-Fri 9-5 and expires in 30 days.
steps: # time restrictions via PAM (pam_time) or the IdP's conditional access policy
verify: the account self-expires and is time-bound

title: Hardening and secure baselines
objective: Apply hardening techniques to systems and endpoints.

questions.q: "Hardening" a system means:
options: Reducing its attack surface by removing/disabling unneeded features and tightening config
questions.explain: Fewer services, fewer accounts, stricter settings = smaller attack surface.

questions.q: A secure "baseline" is:
options: A defined, approved secure configuration that systems are built and checked against
questions.explain: Tools compare live systems to the baseline and flag drift.

questions.q: Disabling unused services helps because:
options: Every running service is a potential entry point
questions.explain: Close ports and stop daemons you do not need.

questions.q: Why change default credentials during hardening?
options: Default usernames/passwords are publicly known and widely attacked
To make login harder for admins
questions.explain: Default creds on routers, cameras and databases are a top breach cause.

questions.q: Application allow-listing (whitelisting) means:
options: Only approved programs may run; everything else is blocked
Blocking a list of bad programs
questions.explain: It is stronger than block-listing but needs maintenance.

questions.q: Full-disk encryption on a laptop protects mainly against:
options: Data theft if the device is lost or stolen
questions.explain: BitLocker/LUKS make the disk unreadable without the key.

questions.q: What is "configuration drift"?
options: Systems gradually diverging from the approved secure baseline over time
questions.explain: Automated config management (Ansible, etc.) corrects drift.

questions.q: A host-based firewall differs from a network firewall because it:
options: Runs on and protects a single host
questions.explain: Defense in depth uses both.

questions.q: On Linux, list every service set to start at boot so you can disable extras.
questions.explain: Disable what you do not need with systemctl disable --now.

labs.title: Build a hardening checklist
labs.scenario: Write a 6-item hardening checklist for a new Linux server, then apply two of the items.
steps: # 1 update all packages  2 disable unused services  3 SSH: no root, keys only
# 4 host firewall: default deny inbound  5 change defaults  6 enable logging/auditd
verify: two items are actually applied

labs.title: Verify against a baseline
labs.scenario: Use a script to check three baseline rules: root SSH disabled, firewall running, and no empty-password accounts.
verify: all three checks pass or you can fix the failures

title: Monitoring, logging and SIEM
objective: Use logs and security monitoring to detect issues.

questions.q: What does a SIEM do?
options: Collects, correlates and alerts on security events from many sources
questions.explain: Security Information and Event Management centralizes logs for detection and investigation.

questions.q: "Log aggregation" means:
options: Gathering logs from many systems into one central place
questions.explain: Central logs survive even if an attacker wipes a host's local logs.

questions.q: Why keep time synchronized (NTP) across systems?
options: So log timestamps line up, making correlation and investigation possible
questions.explain: Skewed clocks make it nearly impossible to reconstruct an incident timeline.

questions.q: What is an IoC (Indicator of Compromise)?
options: An artifact (hash, IP, domain, filename) that suggests a system was breached
questions.explain: Threat feeds share IoCs so defenders can search their environment.

questions.q: "False positive" in an alert means:
options: The tool alerted, but nothing malicious actually happened
The tool missed a real attack
A user typed the wrong password
questions.explain: A false negative is worse: a real attack that produced no alert.

questions.q: NetFlow / flow data is useful because it:
options: Records who talked to whom, when and how much — without full packet contents
questions.explain: Great for spotting beaconing and data exfiltration patterns.

questions.q: What is "alert fatigue"?
options: Analysts becoming desensitized by too many (often low-value) alerts
questions.explain: Tuning rules and prioritizing reduces missed real alerts.

questions.q: A SOAR platform adds what to a SOC?
options: Automation and orchestration of repetitive response tasks (playbooks)
questions.explain: Security Orchestration, Automation and Response speeds up containment.

questions.q: On Linux, follow the auth log live to watch login events during an investigation.
questions.explain: Watch for repeated failures or logins at odd hours.

labs.title: Hunt failed logins
labs.scenario: On a Linux host, count failed SSH logins and list the top source IPs.
steps: journalctl -u sshd --since today | grep -i 'failed password' | wc -l
journalctl -u sshd --since today | grep -oE 'from [0-9.]+' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
verify: you can name the noisiest source IP

labs.title: Centralize a log (concept + practice)
labs.scenario: Explain why central logging matters, then forward this host's logs to a file that an attacker on the host cannot easily reach, and confirm entries arrive.
steps: # central logging survives host compromise and enables correlation
verify: the test event is recorded

labs.title: Write a simple detection rule
labs.scenario: Describe a detection rule for "possible brute force": 10+ failed SSH logins from one IP in 5 minutes, then what response it should trigger.
steps: # response: alert SOC + auto-block the IP (firewall) for 1 hour
verify: the rule has a clear condition and action

title: Firewalls, IDS/IPS and network security tools
objective: Configure and interpret common security appliances.

questions.q: What is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?
options: An IDS detects and alerts; an IPS can also block the traffic inline
questions.explain: IPS sits inline and can drop packets; IDS observes a copy and warns.

questions.q: A "next-generation firewall" (NGFW) adds what over a traditional firewall?
options: Application awareness, IPS, and often user identity and TLS inspection
questions.explain: It filters by application and content, not just port/IP.

questions.q: A stateful firewall differs from a stateless one because it:
options: Tracks the state of connections and allows return traffic automatically
questions.explain: Stateless filters each packet in isolation; stateful understands sessions.

questions.q: A WAF specifically protects:
options: Web applications from attacks like SQL injection and XSS
questions.explain: A Web Application Firewall inspects HTTP requests.

questions.q: Signature-based detection catches:
options: Known threats matching a defined pattern
questions.explain: Anomaly/behavior-based detection is needed for unknown (zero-day) threats.

questions.q: A network "tap" or SPAN port is used to:
options: Copy traffic to a monitoring/IDS tool without disrupting it
questions.explain: It feeds the IDS a mirror of the traffic.

questions.q: "Fail-closed" vs "fail-open" for a security device: fail-closed means:
options: If the device fails, traffic is blocked (security over availability)
questions.explain: Choose based on whether availability or security matters more for that link.

questions.q: Port security on a switch limits:
options: Which/how many MAC addresses may use a switch port
questions.explain: It helps stop rogue devices and MAC flooding.

questions.q: Scan your own lab host to see which TCP ports are open (authorized use only).
questions.explain: Only scan systems you own or are authorized to test.

labs.title: Read firewall logs
labs.scenario: On a Linux host with firewalld, enable logging of denied packets and generate one, then find it.
steps: # from another host, hit a closed port, then:
verify: a blocked connection appears in the log

labs.title: Tune a noisy rule (concept)
labs.scenario: An IDS fires 500 alerts/day for a benign internal scanner. Describe how to reduce the noise without going blind.
steps: # add a tuned exception for the scanner's known IP + scan signature
# keep alerting if that IP does something outside its normal pattern
# document the exception so it can be reviewed
verify: real threats from that host would still alert

title: Incident response
objective: Apply the incident-response process and its phases.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the incident-response phases (NIST)?
options: Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment, Eradication & Recovery, Lessons Learned
questions.explain: Preparation comes first; lessons learned closes the loop.

questions.q: "Containment" aims to:
options: Stop the incident from spreading while preserving evidence
questions.explain: Isolate hosts, block C2, disable accounts — but keep evidence intact.

questions.q: Eradication means:
options: Removing the threat (malware, backdoors, compromised accounts) from the environment
questions.explain: After eradication comes recovery (restoring clean systems).

questions.q: Why is a "lessons learned" meeting important?
options: It improves future preparation and prevents repeat incidents
It is legally required to skip
questions.explain: Update playbooks, controls, and training based on what happened.

questions.q: A "runbook" or "playbook" is:
options: A step-by-step procedure for responding to a specific incident type
questions.explain: Playbooks make response fast and consistent.

questions.q: "Tabletop exercise" means:
options: A discussion-based drill walking through a hypothetical incident
questions.explain: It tests the plan and people without touching real systems.

questions.q: During an incident, who typically declares the incident and coordinates?
questions.explain: Clear roles prevent chaos during response.

questions.q: Why avoid immediately powering off a compromised machine?
options: You may lose volatile evidence in RAM (running processes, keys, connections)
It is faster to leave on
questions.explain: Consider isolating from the network first, then capture memory if needed.

questions.q: On Linux, quickly capture the current network connections and processes for evidence.
questions.explain: Also grab `ps aux` and running services before changing anything.

labs.title: Run a mini IR
labs.scenario: A workstation is beaconing to a bad IP. Walk through the five phases in one line each for this case.
steps: # Detect/Analyze: confirm beacon in flow logs, identify process
# Contain: isolate host from network, block IP at firewall
# Eradicate/Recover: remove malware/persistence, re-image, restore data
# Lessons: how did it get in? add control + training
verify: each phase has a concrete action for this case

labs.title: Preserve volatile evidence
labs.scenario: On a suspect Linux host, collect volatile data in the right order (most volatile first) without rebooting.
steps: # then image memory/disk with proper tools before shutdown
verify: you captured connections and processes before touching the disk

labs.title: Order of volatility
labs.scenario: List the order you would collect evidence from most to least volatile.
steps: # 4 running processes  5 disk  6 remote logs / backups  7 archival media
verify: your order matches order-of-volatility

title: Digital forensics
objective: Apply forensic concepts: chain of custody, acquisition, integrity.

questions.q: "Chain of custody" documents:
options: Who handled evidence, when, and what they did — to keep it admissible
The network path of an attack
questions.explain: A broken chain of custody can make evidence unusable in court.

questions.q: Why hash evidence before and after acquisition?
options: To prove the copy is identical to the original and was not altered
questions.explain: Matching hashes demonstrate integrity of the forensic image.

questions.q: What is a "write blocker"?
options: A device/tool that lets you read a drive without changing it
questions.explain: It preserves the original evidence during acquisition.

questions.q: "Legal hold" means:
options: Preserving relevant data because litigation or investigation is anticipated
questions.explain: Normal deletion/retention is suspended for the relevant data.

questions.q: Which is the best practice for forensic analysis?
options: Work on a verified copy (image), never the original evidence
questions.explain: You keep the original pristine and analyze the image.

questions.q: "Order of volatility" tells you to collect first:
options: The most volatile data (RAM, network state) before it disappears
questions.explain: Data in memory vanishes on power loss.

questions.q: e-Discovery refers to:
options: Identifying and producing electronic evidence for legal proceedings
questions.explain: It ties into legal hold and data retention.

questions.q: Metadata in a file can reveal:
options: Author, timestamps, GPS, device info useful in an investigation
questions.explain: Timestamps and authorship often matter in forensics.

questions.q: Create a verified image of a file/partition and record its hash for the evidence log.
questions.explain: Record the hash immediately after imaging; re-verify before analysis.

labs.title: Practice evidence integrity
labs.scenario: Image a small file, hash the original and the copy, and show they match; then log it as a chain-of-custody entry.
steps: # add: date, collector name, source, method to custody.log
verify: both hashes match and the log has who/when/what

labs.title: Extract file metadata
labs.scenario: Pull timestamps and metadata from a file as an investigator would.
steps: # if available: exiftool suspicious.jpg  (author, GPS, camera, timestamps)
verify: you can report at least three metadata fields

labs.title: Write a chain-of-custody form
labs.scenario: Draft the fields a chain-of-custody form must contain.
steps: # case ID, item description, collected by, date/time, location
# hash value, transferred to (name/sig), reason, storage location
verify: the form would survive a courtroom challenge

title: Resilience, backups and recovery
objective: Apply resilience and recovery concepts (RTO, RPO, backup types).

questions.q: What does RTO (Recovery Time Objective) define?
options: The maximum acceptable time to restore a service after an outage
How much data you can lose
questions.explain: RTO = "how fast must we be back?"

questions.q: What does RPO (Recovery Point Objective) define?
options: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time
questions.explain: RPO = "how much data can we afford to lose?" It drives backup frequency.

questions.q: A full backup:
options: Copies all selected data every time
Copies only changes since the last full
questions.explain: Simple to restore but large and slow.

questions.q: An incremental backup copies:
options: Only data changed since the last backup of any type
Changes since the last full only
questions.explain: Fast backups, but restore needs the full plus every increment in order.

questions.q: A differential backup copies:
options: All changes since the last FULL backup
Only changes since the last backup
questions.explain: Restore needs just the full plus the latest differential.

questions.q: The "3-2-1" backup rule means:
options: 3 copies, on 2 different media, with 1 copy off-site
questions.explain: A modern variant adds "1 offline/immutable" to survive ransomware.

questions.q: High availability (HA) is achieved with:
options: Redundancy and failover so service continues if a component fails
questions.explain: Clusters, load balancers, and redundant power/network provide HA.

questions.q: Why test backups regularly?
options: An untested backup may be corrupt or incomplete when you need it
questions.explain: "You don't have a backup until you've restored it."

questions.q: On Linux, create a compressed, dated backup of /etc for safekeeping.
questions.explain: Store a copy off-site and test the restore.

labs.title: Choose RTO/RPO
labs.scenario: For an online store's order database, propose an RTO and RPO and the backup strategy that meets them.
steps: # RPO 15 min -> transaction log backups every 15 min (or replication)
# RTO 1 hr -> warm standby + tested restore runbook
verify: the backup frequency matches the RPO

labs.title: Backup and verify restore
labs.scenario: Back up a directory, delete a file, and restore just that file to prove the backup works.
verify: the file is restored from backup

labs.title: Plan for ransomware resilience
labs.scenario: List the backup properties that let you recover from ransomware without paying.
steps: # off-site + offline/immutable copy attackers can't reach or encrypt
# versioned backups (restore to a point before infection)
verify: the plan survives an attacker with domain admin

title: Secure protocols and services
objective: Select secure protocols and replace insecure ones.

questions.q: Which protocol securely replaces Telnet for remote administration?
questions.explain: Telnet sends everything in plaintext; SSH is encrypted.

questions.q: HTTPS uses which protocol to encrypt web traffic?
questions.explain: Modern HTTPS uses TLS 1.2/1.3; SSL is deprecated.

questions.q: Which is the secure way to transfer files?
options: SFTP or FTPS (encrypted), not plain FTP
questions.explain: SFTP runs over SSH; FTPS adds TLS to FTP.

questions.q: Which protocol secures email transport between servers?
questions.explain: Also use IMAPS/POP3S for clients, and SPF/DKIM/DMARC for authenticity.

questions.q: SNMPv3 improves on earlier versions by adding:
questions.explain: SNMPv1/v2c send community strings in plaintext.

questions.q: DNSSEC provides:
options: Integrity/authenticity of DNS records via digital signatures
questions.explain: It stops forged records; DoH/DoT add confidentiality.

questions.q: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
questions.explain: 80 = HTTP, 22 = SSH, 25 = SMTP, 443 = HTTPS.

questions.q: LDAPS secures directory queries by:
questions.explain: Plain LDAP (389) exposes directory traffic; LDAPS uses 636.

questions.q: Test whether a mail server offers STARTTLS encryption.
questions.explain: If TLS negotiates, the server supports encrypted mail transport.

labs.title: Replace insecure services
labs.scenario: For a legacy setup using Telnet, FTP, and HTTP, name the secure replacement and the port for each.
verify: each insecure service has a secure, encrypted replacement

labs.title: Verify TLS version and ciphers
labs.scenario: Check which TLS versions and ciphers a web server accepts and flag any weak ones.
verify: you can state whether TLS 1.0/1.1 are (insecurely) enabled

title: Wireless and mobile security
objective: Secure wireless networks and mobile/endpoint devices.

questions.q: Which is the strongest common Wi-Fi security standard?
questions.explain: WEP is broken; WPA2 is okay; WPA3 is current best (SAE handshake).

questions.q: Why is WEP considered insecure?
options: Its weak RC4/IV design lets attackers recover the key quickly
questions.explain: WEP should never be used; it can be cracked in minutes.

questions.q: WPA2-Enterprise differs from WPA2-Personal by using:
options: 802.1X/RADIUS for per-user authentication instead of a shared passphrase
questions.explain: Enterprise gives each user unique credentials and easy revocation.

questions.q: Hiding the SSID (network name) provides:
options: Very little real security (it is easily discovered)
questions.explain: It is "security by obscurity," not a real control.

questions.q: What is MDM (Mobile Device Management) used for?
options: Enforcing security policy on mobile devices (encryption, PIN, remote wipe)
questions.explain: MDM/UEM manages and secures fleets of devices.

questions.q: "BYOD" introduces risk because:
options: Personal devices are outside full corporate control yet access company data
questions.explain: Containerization separates work and personal data on BYOD.

questions.q: A captive portal is:
options: A web page that forces authentication/acceptance before granting network access
questions.explain: Common on guest Wi-Fi; not a strong security control by itself.

questions.q: Remote wipe is important because:
options: A lost/stolen device's data can be erased to prevent exposure
questions.explain: Paired with full-device encryption and a screen lock.

questions.q: Scan for nearby Wi-Fi networks and their security type (your own area, lawful use).
questions.explain: Note which networks still use WEP/WPA vs WPA2/WPA3.

labs.title: Secure a home/office AP (checklist)
labs.scenario: Write the settings you would apply to a wireless router to secure it.
steps: # WPA3 (or WPA2-AES) with a long passphrase
# change default admin password; disable WPS
verify: a war-driver gains nothing easy

labs.title: Enterprise Wi-Fi design (concept)
labs.scenario: Explain how WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise authenticates a user and why it beats a shared key for a company.
steps: # client -> AP -> RADIUS (802.1X/EAP) validates the user's own credentials/cert
# unique creds: revoke one user without changing everyone's password
verify: you can describe the 802.1X flow at a high level

title: Data protection and DLP
objective: Classify data and apply protection controls.

questions.q: Data classification (public, internal, confidential, restricted) exists to:
options: Apply the right level of protection based on sensitivity
questions.explain: You spend the strongest controls on the most sensitive data.

questions.q: "Data at rest" refers to:
options: Data stored on disk/media (protected mainly by encryption)
questions.explain: At rest = storage; in transit = network; in use = memory/processing.

questions.q: "Data in transit" is best protected by:
questions.explain: TLS/IPsec protect data as it crosses the network.

questions.q: What does a DLP system do?
options: Detects and blocks sensitive data from leaving the organization
questions.explain: Data Loss Prevention inspects email, uploads, and endpoints for regulated data.

questions.q: "Tokenization" protects data by:
options: Replacing sensitive values with non-sensitive tokens mapped in a secure vault
questions.explain: Common for payment card data; the real value never leaves the vault.

questions.q: "Data masking" is used to:
options: Hide parts of data (e.g., show only last 4 digits) for non-privileged views
questions.explain: Useful in test environments and customer-service screens.

questions.q: A data "owner" is responsible for:
options: Classifying the data and deciding who may access it
questions.explain: The custodian implements the controls the owner defines.

questions.q: "Right to be forgotten" comes from which kind of regulation?
questions.explain: Data-subject rights require you to locate and delete personal data on request.

questions.q: Find files that may contain card numbers before they leak (simple DLP-style scan).
questions.explain: A real DLP tool adds validation (Luhn check) and context.

labs.title: Classify and label data
labs.scenario: For a folder with an HR salary sheet, a public brochure, and a customer list, assign a classification and one control each.
steps: # salary sheet -> Confidential -> encrypt + restrict to HR group
# brochure -> Public -> integrity check, no confidentiality needed
# customer list -> Restricted (PII) -> encrypt, DLP, access logging
verify: each item's controls match its sensitivity

labs.title: Protect data three ways
labs.scenario: Demonstrate protection for data at rest, in transit, and in use (conceptually) on one file.
steps: # in transit: send over scp/TLS, never plain FTP
# in use: restrict process privileges + memory, limit who can open it
verify: you addressed all three states

title: Physical security
objective: Apply physical security controls.

questions.q: A mantrap (access control vestibule) prevents:
options: Tailgating, by allowing one person through at a time
questions.explain: Two interlocking doors stop a second person slipping in.

questions.q: Why place security cameras (CCTV) at entrances?
options: To deter and to detect/record who enters
questions.explain: Visible cameras deter; recordings provide detective evidence.

questions.q: A bollard is used to:
options: Physically block vehicles from ramming a building
questions.explain: Physical, preventive control against vehicle attacks.

questions.q: "Faraday cage" protects against:
questions.explain: Used for shielding sensitive equipment and preventing signal leakage.

questions.q: Biometric access control is which authentication factor?
questions.explain: Fingerprints, iris, face. Watch for false accept/reject rates.

questions.q: A "proximity badge" is which factor?
questions.explain: Combine with a PIN (know) for MFA at the door.

questions.q: Why use security lighting and clear sightlines?
options: They deter intruders and improve camera/guard effectiveness
questions.explain: Environmental design (CPTED) reduces hiding spots.

questions.q: A "honeyfile" or honeytoken is:
options: A decoy file/credential that alerts defenders when touched
questions.explain: Any access to it strongly implies an intruder.

labs.title: Design layered physical security
labs.scenario: For a small server room, list controls from the perimeter inward (defense in depth).
steps: # building: badge + PIN door, reception, visitor logs
# server room: mantrap, separate badge, camera, locked racks
verify: each layer backs up the others

labs.title: FAR vs FRR (concept)
labs.scenario: Explain false acceptance rate and false rejection rate and which is worse for a high-security door.
steps: # FAR: wrongly admits an impostor (security risk)
# FRR: wrongly rejects a valid user (annoyance)
# high security: tune to lower FAR even if FRR rises
verify: you can state the trade-off

title: Governance, policies and standards
objective: Summarize governance, policies, standards and frameworks.

questions.q: What is the difference between a policy and a procedure?
options: A policy states what/why (high level); a procedure states step-by-step how
questions.explain: Standards and guidelines sit between them.

questions.q: An Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) defines:
options: How employees may use company systems and data
questions.explain: Users typically sign it during onboarding.

questions.q: A "standard" (vs a policy) is:
options: A mandatory specific rule that supports a policy (e.g., "AES-256 for encryption")
questions.explain: Guidelines are recommended, not mandatory; standards are mandatory.

questions.q: What is a security framework used for?
options: A structured set of best practices to build and measure a security program
questions.explain: Examples: NIST CSF, ISO 27001, CIS Controls.

questions.q: "Separation of duties" prevents fraud by:
options: Requiring more than one person to complete a sensitive task
questions.explain: No single person can both request and approve a payment, for example.

questions.q: "Mandatory vacation" and "job rotation" are controls that:
options: Help detect fraud and reduce dependence on one person
questions.explain: Fraud often surfaces when the usual person is away.

questions.q: Onboarding and offboarding processes matter because:
options: They ensure access is granted correctly and fully removed when someone leaves
questions.explain: Orphaned accounts of ex-employees are a major risk.

questions.q: What is "due care" vs "due diligence"?
options: Due diligence is investigating/planning; due care is acting on it responsibly
questions.explain: Diligence = doing your homework; care = the ongoing responsible action.

labs.title: Write an access-control policy snippet
labs.scenario: Draft three policy statements for user account management (creation, review, removal).
steps: # Accounts are created only via approved onboarding tickets with manager sign-off.
# Access is reviewed quarterly; unused/excess access is revoked.
# Accounts are disabled within 1 hour of termination.
verify: each statement is enforceable and auditable

labs.title: Map to a framework
labs.scenario: Pick three CIS Controls (or NIST CSF functions) and give one action your org would take for each.
steps: # e.g. NIST CSF: Identify -> asset inventory
verify: each function has a concrete action

title: Risk management
objective: Apply risk-management concepts and calculations.

questions.q: What is "risk" in security terms?
options: The likelihood of a threat exploiting a vulnerability and the resulting impact
questions.explain: Risk = likelihood x impact, roughly.

questions.q: The four risk-response strategies are:
questions.explain: Transfer often means buying insurance; mitigate means adding controls.

questions.q: Buying cyber-insurance is an example of risk:
questions.explain: You shift the financial impact to a third party.

questions.q: "Residual risk" is:
options: The risk that remains after controls are applied
questions.explain: You cannot usually reach zero; leadership accepts the residual.

questions.q: SLE x ARO equals:
questions.explain: Single Loss Expectancy x Annual Rate of Occurrence = expected yearly loss.

questions.q: If an asset is worth $10,000 and an incident destroys 50% of it, the SLE is:
questions.explain: SLE = Asset Value x Exposure Factor = 10,000 x 0.5.

questions.q: A "risk register" is:
options: A living document listing risks, owners, and treatment status
questions.explain: It tracks each risk from identification to closure.

questions.q: Qualitative risk analysis uses:
options: Ratings like high/medium/low rather than exact numbers
questions.explain: Quantitative analysis uses numbers (SLE/ALE); qualitative uses judgment scales.

labs.title: Calculate ALE
labs.scenario: A server worth $20,000 faces a flood that would destroy 25% of it, expected once every 4 years. Compute SLE, ARO, and ALE.
steps: # ALE = SLE x ARO = 5000 x 0.25 = $1,250 per year
verify: a control costing < $1,250/yr that removes this risk is justified

labs.title: Build a mini risk register
labs.scenario: Add three risks for a web app, each with likelihood, impact, response strategy, and owner.
steps: # SQLi -> High/High -> Mitigate (WAF+prepared stmts) -> Dev lead
verify: each row is complete and actionable

title: Third-party and vendor risk
objective: Manage supply-chain and third-party risk.

questions.q: Why assess third-party vendors' security?
options: Their weaknesses can become your breach (supply-chain risk)
questions.explain: A vendor with access to your data extends your attack surface.

questions.q: An SLA (Service Level Agreement) defines:
options: The measurable service levels a vendor must meet (e.g., uptime)
questions.explain: Include security requirements and penalties in the SLA.

questions.q: An MOU/MOA is:
options: A (often non-binding) agreement outlining intentions between parties
questions.explain: It sets expectations before a formal contract.

questions.q: A BPA (Business Partners Agreement) governs:
options: The relationship and responsibilities between business partners
questions.explain: It clarifies liability, data handling, and responsibilities.

questions.q: "Right to audit" clauses let you:
options: Verify a vendor's security controls yourself or via a third party
questions.explain: Without it, you rely only on the vendor's word.

questions.q: A SOC 2 report tells you:
options: How well a vendor's controls meet security/availability criteria
questions.explain: It is independent assurance about a service provider's controls.

questions.q: "Vendor lock-in" is a risk because:
options: It makes leaving a provider costly/difficult, reducing your options
questions.explain: Consider exit strategy and data portability up front.

questions.q: End-of-life (EOL) hardware/software from a vendor means:
options: No more security updates, so risk rises over time
questions.explain: Plan replacement before EOL; isolate if you cannot.

labs.title: Vendor security questionnaire
labs.scenario: Write five questions you would ask a SaaS vendor before storing customer data with them.
steps: # Where is data stored, and is it encrypted at rest/in transit?
# Do you have SOC 2 / ISO 27001? Can we see it?
# How do you handle breach notification and in what timeframe?
# What is your access control and MFA posture for staff?
# What is our data export/deletion process on exit?
verify: the answers would materially change your decision

labs.title: Assess supply-chain risk
labs.scenario: For a software dependency your app pulls from the internet, list three controls to reduce supply-chain risk.
steps: # use a private/proxy registry and scan dependencies for CVEs
# review before upgrading; monitor for compromised packages
verify: a poisoned update would be caught before deployment

title: Audits, assessments and testing
objective: Compare security assessments, audits and testing types.

questions.q: A vulnerability scan differs from a penetration test because it:
options: Identifies weaknesses but does not exploit them
questions.explain: A pen test goes further and proves impact by exploiting.

questions.q: "Black box" penetration testing means the tester:
options: Has no prior internal knowledge of the target
questions.explain: White box = full knowledge; gray box = partial.

questions.q: The "rules of engagement" in a pen test define:
options: Scope, timing, allowed techniques, and contacts — the authorized boundaries
questions.explain: Testing outside the authorized scope can be illegal.

questions.q: An internal audit's main purpose is to:
options: Independently verify that controls exist and work as intended
questions.explain: Audits check compliance with policy/standards.

questions.q: "Attestation" in an audit is:
options: A formal statement that controls were reviewed and meet criteria
questions.explain: Often provided to customers as assurance.

questions.q: A "red team" exercise:
options: Simulates a real adversary to test detection and response, not just find bugs
questions.explain: The "blue team" defends; "purple" is the two collaborating.

questions.q: Why do a "bug bounty" program?
options: To pay external researchers to responsibly report vulnerabilities
questions.explain: It widens your testing pool under defined rules.

questions.q: A compliance scan checks systems against:
options: A required standard/benchmark (e.g., PCI DSS, CIS)
questions.explain: It reports gaps you must remediate for compliance.

questions.q: Run an authorized vulnerability-style scan of your lab host with nmap scripts.
questions.explain: Authorized targets only; interpret results and prioritize by severity + exposure.

labs.title: Plan a penetration test
labs.scenario: Draft the rules of engagement for testing a single web app: scope, window, allowed/forbidden actions, and emergency contact.
steps: # scope: app.example.com only, no DoS, no social engineering
# forbidden: data destruction, pivoting to other systems
# contact: on-call number to stop the test immediately
verify: the ROE keeps the test legal and safe

labs.title: Compare assessment types
labs.scenario: In one line each, distinguish vulnerability scan, penetration test, audit, and red-team exercise.
steps: # vuln scan: automated find weaknesses (no exploit)
# pen test: exploit to prove impact within scope
# red team: adversary simulation to test detection/response
verify: you can pick the right one for a given goal

title: Automation, orchestration and secure ops
objective: Apply automation to security operations securely.

questions.q: A key benefit of automation in security operations is:
options: Consistent, fast, repeatable responses that reduce human error
questions.explain: Playbooks in SOAR auto-triage and contain common incidents.

questions.q: A risk of over-automation is:
options: A flawed script can cause damage at scale, quickly
questions.explain: Guardrails, approvals, and testing keep automation safe.

questions.q: Storing secrets (API keys, passwords) in code is bad because:
options: Anyone with the code gets the secret; use a secrets manager instead
questions.explain: Use a vault and inject secrets at runtime.

questions.q: "Idempotent" automation means:
options: Running it repeatedly yields the same safe end state
questions.explain: Configuration tools like Ansible aim for idempotency.

questions.q: CI/CD security ("shift left") means:
options: Adding security testing early in the development pipeline
questions.explain: Catch flaws before production with SAST/DAST and dependency scans.

questions.q: A "least-privilege" service account for automation should:
options: Have only the permissions the task needs, and be monitored
questions.explain: Over-privileged automation accounts are prime targets.

questions.q: Why sign your scripts/artifacts in a pipeline?
options: To ensure integrity and that only trusted code runs (supply-chain defense)
questions.explain: Signature verification stops tampered artifacts from deploying.

questions.q: Store a secret in an environment variable for a script instead of hard-coding it (lab).
questions.explain: Better: use a real secrets manager; never commit secrets to Git.

labs.title: Automate a safe check
labs.scenario: Write a short script that checks disk usage and alerts (logs) if over 80%, and make it idempotent.
verify: running it twice does not cause harm

labs.title: Find hard-coded secrets
labs.scenario: Scan a code directory for likely secrets before committing.
verify: you can spot secrets that should move to a vault

title: Endpoint and email security
objective: Protect endpoints and email against modern threats.

questions.q: EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) provides:
options: Continuous monitoring, detection, and response on endpoints
questions.explain: EDR sees behavior and enables remote investigation/containment.

questions.q: How does EDR differ from traditional antivirus?
options: It focuses on behavior/telemetry and response, not just known-signature files
questions.explain: AV catches known malware; EDR catches suspicious behavior and enables hunting.

questions.q: SPF, DKIM and DMARC together help:
options: Verify email sender authenticity and reduce spoofing/phishing
questions.explain: SPF authorizes senders, DKIM signs messages, DMARC sets policy + reporting.

questions.q: Application allow-listing on endpoints:
questions.explain: Strong against unknown malware, but needs upkeep.

questions.q: "Sandboxing" a suspicious attachment means:
options: Detonating it in an isolated environment to observe behavior safely
questions.explain: Email gateways and EDR use sandboxes to catch unknown malware.

questions.q: A key control against ransomware on endpoints is:
options: EDR + least privilege + tested offline backups + patching
questions.explain: Layered defenses reduce both the chance and the impact.

questions.q: "Host-based intrusion prevention" (HIPS) does what?
options: Blocks malicious behavior on the endpoint itself
questions.explain: Complements EDR and host firewall.

questions.q: Email attachment "content disarm and reconstruction" (CDR):
options: Strips active content and rebuilds a safe version of the file
questions.explain: It removes macros/scripts while keeping the document usable.

questions.q: On Linux, check a downloaded file's type before opening it, to avoid disguised executables.
questions.explain: If "PDF" is actually an executable or script, do not run it.

labs.title: Configure email authentication (concept)
labs.scenario: Write the DNS records (conceptually) for SPF, DKIM and DMARC for example.com and say what each does.
verify: you can explain how the three work together

labs.title: Endpoint hardening quick win
labs.scenario: On a Linux endpoint, ensure automatic security updates are considered and the firewall is on, and verify.
steps: dnf install -y dnf-automatic 2>/dev/null; systemctl enable --now dnf-automatic.timer 2>/dev/null || true
verify: firewall is active and update automation is considered

title: Security+ exam-day strategy
objective: Approach the SY0-701 exam and its performance-based questions.

questions.q: How many questions and how long is the SY0-701 exam (approx)?
questions.explain: It mixes multiple-choice and performance-based questions (PBQs).

questions.q: What is the SY0-701 passing score?
questions.explain: It is scaled, so it is not a simple percentage.

questions.q: Performance-based questions (PBQs) usually ask you to:
options: Perform a task or solve a scenario (drag-drop, configure, analyze output)
questions.explain: Many test-takers skip PBQs first, then return with remaining time.

questions.q: A good strategy for a hard PBQ early in the exam is:
options: Flag it, move on, and return after answering the quick multiple-choice items
questions.explain: Bank the easy points first; PBQs can eat your clock.

questions.q: When two answers look correct, choose the one that is:
options: BEST/MOST secure and most directly addresses the question asked
questions.explain: CompTIA wants the best answer, not just a correct-sounding one.

questions.q: "MOST likely" and "BEST" in a question mean you should:
options: Rank the options and pick the strongest fit, even if others are partly right
questions.explain: These keywords signal more than one option is plausible.

questions.q: If you do not know an answer, you should:
options: Eliminate wrong options, then make your best guess (no penalty for guessing)
questions.explain: There is no penalty, so never leave a blank.

questions.q: The best way to be ready for PBQs is to:
options: Practice hands-on tasks (firewall rules, log reading, hardening) beforehand
questions.explain: That is exactly why the Labs and command drills in this app matter.
